primaries.primaryEn: The king asks with folded hands: tell me fully — what is Her true form, and in what way should I worship Her? (Verses 1–2, Hindi.) In simple words Suratha the king begs the sage: show me exactly who the Mother is and how I should serve Her — hold nothing back from surrendered me.

The sage speaks: this mystery is supreme, not fit to be told — yet since you are a devotee, O king among men, nothing of mine is untellable to you. (Verse 3.) Combined with Guptavatī's opening key to the whole mystery: 'you are a devotee' means devotee of both Goddess and guru. At the book's start the truth-form was told — Brahman as religion itself, named by the word Caṇḍikā, the worshipped reality — and its three branch-forms: Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, Mahāsarasvatī. So Caṇḍikā the fourth is the Whole itself, religion-shaped, beyond qualities — yet counted fifth. Since telling the three branches nearly tells their undivided Whole, the fourth, the text wordlessly drops the Whole and points instead to one of the branches as equal to the fourth in shelter-giving — calling it three-qualitied, formless, unseeable, dwelling within the three descents. (Continued next.)

Taking the pure-goodness Whole aside from the three, the text begins telling creation from one of the three alone — how from it the other two streamed out. (Verse 3, Guptavatī completion.) In simple words the method is shown: keep the fourth (the Whole) quietly aside, and tell the whole creation-story through Mahālakṣmī, from whom the other two goddesses flow.

The sage said to the king: this mystery, asked by you, is top-secret — worth telling only in secret. But since you are a devotee, nothing is untellable to me for you. (Verse 3, Hindi.) In simple words the teacher tests and then trusts: this wisdom is too precious for casual ears, but a true devotee may hear everything.

Mahālakṣmī, first of all, three-qualitied, supreme Lady — of seen-and-unseen form, She stands pervading everything. (Verse 4.) Combined with the commentaries: 'first of all' — the three-qualitied Whole of goodness-passion-darkness faces is itself the first cause of the whole expanse, say some; others say Mahālakṣmī here is not one of the three branches but another name of the fourth, Caṇḍikā Herself — 'Śivā named Śakti, seated on Sadāśiva's lap, famed as Mahālakṣmī, rich in all gods' qualities,' says the Śiva Purāṇa. Not so, answers Guptavatī: the Mahālakṣmī inside the sacrifices stands apart, being passion-heavy, praised through ten names, with no telling of the other two — so supplying extra words just to force that reading is painful twisting. 'Seen' means with qualities, 'unseen' means without qualities — Her grasping never shows, so She is called unseen; as the Goddess-Atharva-Top scripture says, She is knowledge whose object is Herself — knowledge that kills mere mind-knowledge. For 'I know this pot' ends in 'I', and though Brahman is reached by the last mind-wave, It is never reached as a fruit-object — that is the feeling. One book reads 'and twice-born' here.

Knowledge whose object is Herself — never grasped as a fruit-object, though the last mind-wave touches It. (Verse 4, Guptavatī completion.) In simple words the deepest point: you cannot 'know' the Mother the way you know a pot — She is the knowing itself, not a thing to be known.

The three-qualitied supreme Lady Mahālakṣmī, first of all, stands pervading the whole universe in seen and unseen form. (Verse 4, Hindi.) In simple words: before everything, the three-powered great Goddess — visible as the world, invisible as its soul — fills all.

Citron, mace, shield and drinking-cup She holds; serpent, emblem and womb-sign She wears, O king, on the crown. (Verse 5.) In simple words the Mother's four hands hold citron-fruit, mace, shield and wine-cup, while Her crown mysteriously carries serpent, Śiva-mark and Goddess-mark.

Glowing like heated gold, decked in heated-gold ornaments — She filled all that emptiness with Her own glory. (Verse 6.) In simple words: golden-bodied, gold-decked, She poured Her own light into the total void until nothing empty remained.
Seeing all that world empty, the supreme Lady wore another form — of mere darkness only. (Verse 7.) In simple words: looking at the hollow universe, out of Her own dark side She put on a second body.

She became a woman — smooth-dark like collyrium, with fangs lighting Her noble face, wide-eyed, slim-waisted. (Verse 8.) Combined with the commentaries: pointing to the 'seen' — citron means the seed-filled fruit; 'shield' is hide, held in hands, supply that; serpent and the other two She wears on the crown — 'emblem' here is Rudra's male mark, 'womb' Viṣṇu's female mark (for the Veda bids 'fashion a Viṣṇu-womb'), so by leftover logic the serpent must be Brahmā's mark. Thus She shows Herself as Brahmā-Viṣṇu-Rudra in one, male-female in one. Then the 'unseen': at world-dissolution the world rests as seed-habit without gross form — that She pervaded with Her glory, which is pure consciousness, is the sense. And that same Mahālakṣmī ripened further into Mahākālī-hood — 'seeing emptiness' (verses 7–8). The Hindi prayer repeats: O king, four-armed Mahālakṣmī holds citron (sweet-lime fruit), mace, shield and wine-cup, and wears serpent, emblem and womb-marks on the head (5); glowing like heated gold, wearing heated-gold ornaments (continued next).
Glowing like heated gold, wearing heated-gold ornaments, She filled the whole void with Her glory. (Verse 6, Hindi.) In simple words the golden Mother floods the emptiness with light until it shines.

Seeing the whole world hollow, the supreme Lady surely wore a second form from Her dark side only. (Verse 7, Hindi, with old note.) Combined with the old note: from Mahālakṣmī's dark share was born that woman — smooth like collyrium, with out-jutting splitter fangs lighting Her noble face, wide-eyed and slim-bodied. (Verse 8.)

Sword, wine-cup, head and shield-decked, four-armed; wearing a trunk-garland on the chest, a head-garland on the head. (Verse 9.) In simple words the dark Mother's four arms glitter — sword, cup, severed head, shield — with headless trunks garlanding Her chest and a skull-garland on Her head.

To Her, finest of proud ladies, Mahālakṣmī spoke: I give you the names — and yours shall be the deeds. (Verse 10.) In simple words the golden Mother addresses the newly-born dark lady, best of women: I shall give you names, and matching works shall be yours.

Mahāmāyā, Mahākālī, Mahāmārī, hunger, thirst; sleep, craving, the One Heroine, Night-of-death hard to cross. (Verse 11.) Combined with the commentaries: 'head' means the neck-part set on a pole, the skull-staff; 'trunks' are headless bodies — supply 'on the chest'; She wears a trunk-garland on the chest and a head-garland on the head, is the sense. 'To Her spoke' — but some read the first and second persons swapped, making it the dark lady's sentence — wasted effort, that. For the उत्तर-half 'give me name and deed, O Mother, salutation to You' is seen in many books — which rather unjoins it; so some people's case-split reading too is not to be taken. With no question from the goodness-natured one, the name-first answer ahead tells it. (Verses 9–11.) The Hindi prayer repeats: four arms graced with sword, wine-cup, head and shield; trunk-garland on the chest, skull-garland on the head (9). Some books add here an extra verse — the dark finest lady asks Mahālakṣmī: 'give me name and deed, O Mother, salutation to You' — but since most books don't agree, it ranks as inserted. Then Mahālakṣmī to the newly-born finest dark lady: 'I am giving you your names and telling your deeds' (10): Mahāmāyā, Mahākālī, Mahāmārī, hunger, thirst, sleep, craving, One Heroine, death-night and hard-to-cross (11). One book reads 'wearing a head-garland indeed' here.

These are your names, to be proved by your deeds; knowing your deeds through them, whoever studies gains joy. (Verse 12.) In simple words: live these ten names through Your works, and whoever learns Your deeds through them and sings them will taste happiness.

Having thus spoken to Her, Mahālakṣmī, O king, wore another form — by the over-pure quality called goodness, moon-bright. (Verse 13.) In simple words: after naming the dark daughter, Mahālakṣmī Herself put on a second body of purest goodness, glowing like moonlight.

Rosary, goad and lute-book-bearer, She became a lovely woman — and to Her too She gave names. (Verse 14.) Combined with Guptavatī's ten-name soul-meanings from the Kālī Purāṇa (Mahāmāyā: She who keeps the womb-wise being pushed by birth-winds, born wisdom-less, ever yoking him through past-life habits — into delusion, mine-ness, doubt at day's start, then hurling him again and again into anger, checks, greed, then joining him to lust, worry night and day, joylessness and vice-addiction — hence the world-Queen is hailed Great Illusion; and the Devī Purāṇa's name-meaning chapter gives the other names — seek them there). Name-chanting with such meaning-knowledge beforehand is what bears fruit. 'Through them' (verse 12). And that She ripened into Mahāsarasvatī-hood too: 'having spoken to Her' — and the verse 'these are yours' joins to that ten-name set as well. (Verses 13–14.) The Hindi prayer repeats: these ten are your names, to prove true through your deeds in days to come; whoever learns your deeds through them, sings and reflects, will enjoy joy (12). O king, telling the dark Goddess so, Mahālakṣmī wore by purest goodness a second moon-bright form (13). That finest lady held rosary, goad, lute and book in hand — and Mahālakṣmī gave names to Her too (14).

The same ten-name verse joins here too, and the moon-bright second form follows. (Verses 13–14, Guptavatī seal.) In simple words: the name-giving pattern repeats for the bright daughter exactly as for the dark one.

Rosary, goad, lute and book in hand — and Mahālakṣmī gave names to this lady too. (Verse 14, Hindi.) In simple words the bright daughter rises holding prayer-beads, elephant-goad, music and scripture — and receives Her own ten names.

Mahāvidyā, Mahāvāṇī, Bhāratī, Vāk, Sarasvatī; Āryā, Brāhmī, Mahādhenu, Vedagarbhā, Sureśvarī. (Verse 15.) In simple words the ten names of the bright daughter: Great Wisdom, Great Speech, Eloquence, Voice, Flowing One, Noble Lady, Creator's Power, Great Milk-Cow, Veda-Womb, Queen of gods.

Then Mahālakṣmī said to Mahākālī and Sarasvatī: bring forth, O goddesses, a pair each, after your own likeness. (Verse 16.) In simple words the golden Mother commands Her two daughters: each of you create one woman-and-man pair in your own image.

So told, they — Mahālakṣmī Herself created a pair: golden-wombed, lovely, a woman and man on lotus seats. (Verse 17.) In simple words: commanded so, Mahālakṣmī first created a couple Herself — both golden-wombed, beautiful, seated on lotuses, one woman one man.

'O Brahman! O Maker! O Creator! O Holder!' — She called the man; 'O Fortune! O Lotus! O Lovely! O Luck!' — the mother called the woman. (Verse 18.) In simple words the Mother names Her first children: him — Brahman, Maker, Creator, Holder; her — Fortune, Lotus, Lovely, Luck.

Mahākālī and Bhāratī too created a pair, indeed; their forms and names also I tell you. (Verse 19.) In simple words: the dark and bright daughters each made a couple too — and the sage promises to describe all their faces and names.

Blue-throated, red-armed, white-limbed, moon-crested — a man Mahākālī bore, and a fair woman. (Verse 20.) Combined with Guptavatī's grammar: 'in a pair a son and a daughter' — a brother-sister twin. 'Herself' here some explain as 'bearing Her own Śrī-named branch-form' — but for us who say Mahālakṣmī is the branch's very name, no such strain. (Verses 15–20.) The Hindi prayer lists: Mahāvidyā 1, Mahāvāṇī 2, Bhāratī 3, Vāk 4 (with variant notes 5 Sarasvatī, 6 Āryā, 7 Brāhmī, 8 wish-cow, 9 Veda-womb, 10 queen of wisdom — 'these ten shall be your names', verse 15). Then Mahālakṣmī bade Mahākālī and Mahāsarasvatī each bring forth a woman-man pair in their own likeness (16). So told, Mahālakṣmī Herself made a pair — both golden-wombed, lovely, lotus-seated (17). Then Mother Mahālakṣmī addressed the man as Brahman, Maker, Creator, Holder, and the woman as Fortune, Lotus, Lovely, Luck (18). Mahākālī and Mahāsarasvatī each made a pair too — 'their faces and names I tell you, Suratha' (19). Mahākālī bore a blue-throated, red-armed, white-limbed, moon-crested man, and with him a fair woman (20).

The pair-grammar settled: son-daughter, brother-sister twins — and Mahālakṣmī needs no strained reading, since the name is Hers by branch-right. (Verses 15–20, Guptavatī seal.) In simple words the commentator refuses twisted grammar: the golden Mother simply is Mahālakṣmī, and the twins are plainly son and daughter.

Mahākālī bore a blue-throated, red-armed, white-limbed, moon-crested man, and a fair woman with him. (Verse 20, Hindi.) In simple words the dark daughter's children: a moon-crowned blue-throated son with red arms and white limbs, and a fair daughter beside him.

He is Rudra, Śaṅkara, the Still One, the braided, the three-eyed; she is the triple lore, wisdom, wish-cow — speech, letter, note. (Verse 21.) In simple words the twins are named: he — Rudra, Kind-Doer, Stillness, Matted-Locks, Three-Eyes; she — the three Vedas, Learning, Wish-Cow, Language, Letter, Musical Note.
Sarasvatī bore a fair woman and a dark man, O king — their names too I tell you. (Verse 22.) In simple words the bright daughter's twins: a fair daughter and a dark son — hear their names next.

Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Heart-Lord, All-Pervader, Man-Rescuer; Umā, Gaurī, Satī, Caṇḍī, Lovely, Lucky, Blessed. (Verse 23.) In simple words: he is Viṣṇu by five names, she is Umā by seven — the Preserver pair fully named.

Thus the young women at once reached manhood; the eyed ones see it truly — other men, not knowing that, do not. (Verse 24.) Combined with Guptavatī's deep key: 'triple lore and wisdom' — scholarly or not, each is a separate name-pair (verses 21–23). Having made three pairs, since weddings need bride-giving parents and no other men exist but themselves, they themselves took double-form, male-and-female both — 'thus' says so. Manhood Mahālakṣmī reached, Brahmahood Mahākālī, Rudrahood Mahāsarasvatī, Viṣṇuhood — is the sense. For though young women, they hold manhood too — not as two persons, nor half-and-half like the half-woman-lord, but both all-pervading, like sunlight and shade both filling the same bowl of water — that is the feeling. And this form is unseen to flesh-eyes, says 'the eyed': wisdom alone, fed by the teacher's nine-lettered grace, is the true eye — 'not knowing that' reads un-split. (Verse 24.) The Hindi prayer repeats it whole: Rudra-Śaṅkara-Still-Matted-Three-eyed he; triple-lore-wisdom-wish-cow-speech-letter-note she (21); O king, Mahāsarasvatī bore a fair woman and a dark man — hear both their names (22): Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Heart-Lord, All-Pervader, Man-Rescuer he; Umā, Gaurī, Satī, Caṇḍī, Lovely, Lucky, Blessed she (23). Thus the three maidens at once became men too — the eyed (wisdom-given by the teacher) surely see it; others, not knowing this wisdom, cannot see. (24.)

Three maidens became men too — not as split halves but both-wholly, like light and shade filling one bowl — seen only by wisdom-eyes, not flesh-eyes. (Verse 24, Guptavatī seal.) In simple words the mystery's heart: each goddess is fully woman and fully man at once, and only the teacher-opened eye can see it.

To Brahmā Mahālakṣmī gave as wife Trayī; to Rudra, boon-giving Gaurī; and Śrī to Vāsudeva. (Verse 25.) In simple words the three weddings: Brahmā weds Learning, Rudra weds Fair Gaurī, Viṣṇu weds Fortune.
With Svarā joined, Brahmā hatched an egg; potent Rudra split it with Gaurī. (Verse 26.) In simple words: Brahmā with Learning laid the cosmic egg, and mighty Rudra with Fair One broke it open.

Inside the egg, O king, came the whole brood from First-cause — the entire still-and-moving world of five-element stuff. (Verse 27.) In simple words: inside that egg unfolded everything — from root nature through ego and elements (the Sāṅkhya list) — the whole moving-and-unmoving universe.

Keśava with Lakṣmī fed and guarded it; and Mahālakṣmī alone, O king, is held Queen of the lords of all. (Verse 28.) Combined with the commentaries: 'with Svarā joined' means met with triple-lore wisdom; 'that' — the egg-world of root-nature, ego and elements in order, the Sāṅkhya tattva-group (verses 26–27). 'Mahālakṣmī' — both Her formless and formed faces are Hers, not the other two's. So among the three branches, the Mahālakṣmī tinged with passion-chiefly usable two qualities, both-formed-and-formless, is the worshippable — that is the triple group. And to remove the doubt 'why are Mahālakṣmī's ten names barely sung if the branches matter most' — 'She alone' answers: since She alone gives names to the others, endless regress stops at the Giver needing no other giver — that is the 'alone'. The Hindi prayer repeats the weddings and world-making whole: Mahālakṣmī gave Learning to Brahmā, boon-Gaurī to Rudra, Fortune to Vāsudeva (25); with Learning Brahmā laid an egg; potent Rudra with Fair One split it (26); inside, O king, came the root-cause brood — the whole five-element still-moving world (27); then Keśava-Viṣṇu with Lakṣmī fed and guarded it all (and with Fair One the Great Lord later destroyed it all — a verse some books carry but the original here lacks). So, O king, Mahālakṣmī alone stands as Queen of all lords (other books: 'Mahālakṣmī the All-goodness Queen and All-Queen', verse 28).

She alone is formless and formed, bearing many titles; by other names She is to be known — by no other name but names. (Verse 29.) In simple words the seal-verse: formless and formed both, many-named, She is known through names alone — and through no name but names.

Thus ends the Prādhāna mystery. Combined with Guptavatī's grand finale: 'by other names' means by the other two branches' names alone — since the Fourth needs no separate names of Her own, that is the feeling. So with the Fourth quietly set aside, the Mahālakṣmī inside the three branches is the very best — that devotee-pride is the book's own natural intent. Hence the Saptashatī's four hymns: the Goddess-hymn praises the Fourth through the non-difference of Mahākālī and the other two; the other three hymns serve the three quality-faces in turn — that is the fine point. Others say the Fourth alone is worshippable and all three branches are low, and they painfully drag this book to say: Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, Mahāsarasvatī rule the three stories in turn, and the Fourth rules only the nine-lettered — but if the Saptashatī worshipped branches alone and never the Fourth, then the Lakṣmī-Tantra's Indra-dialogue (where ten descents are told from Mahālakṣmī first through Mahākālī to Bhrāmarī, closing with 'supreme is She, firm-set, greatly blest Mahālakṣmī, nature, supreme Lady; for Her praise Brahmā and all gods saw the Goddess-hymn, giver of all wished fruits; chanting it daily, crossing all pains, one wins great lordship; and Her descents with stories Vasiṣṭha told of old to King Suratha of the Svārociṣa age and to the surrendered merchant Samādhi') — all that would clash. For it proves the branch-dwelling Mahālakṣmī's firmness, Her non-difference, the Goddess-hymn's devotion to Her alone, and the three stories' devotion to Her through the branches — clarified by the Fourth Herself. So the whole Saptashatī is Mahālakṣmī wearing non-difference with the Fourth as supreme — which is why 'by one, or by the middle' allows the middle story alone as option for all three stories together — that is the direction. (Verse 29, end of Guptavatī on the Prādhāna mystery.) The Hindi prayer repeats: Mahālakṣmī alone is formless and formed, bearing many names — so She is knowable through those name-forms, and through no single other name. (29.)

Through those very name-forms She is knowable — through no other single name. (Verse 29, Hindi.) In simple words the closing seal: don't hunt for one magic word — know Her through all Her names together.

The sage speaks: the Goddess told as threefold — three-qualitied, dark-natured, goodness-natured — She is called Śarvā, Caṇḍikā, Durgā, Bhadrā, Bhagavatī. (Vaikṛta verse 1.) In simple words the mystery of Her changed (vaikṛta) faces opens: one Mother, three natures — passion-full Mahālakṣmī, dark Mahākālī, bright Mahāsarasvatī — and by five more names She is hailed: with-Śarva, Fierce One, Hard-to-reach, Blessed, Fortuned.

Hari's sleep-yoga, they say, is Mahākālī of dark quality — whom lotus-seated Brahmā praised to kill Madhu-Kaiṭabha. (Verse 2.) In simple words: the sleep that closed Viṣṇu's eyes at world-start is Herself — dark Mahākālī, praised by Brahmā on His lotus when the two demons came to kill Him.

Ten-faced, ten-armed, ten-footed, glowing like collyrium; shining with a vast thirty-eye garland. (Verse 3.) In simple words the dark Mother's awesome arithmetic: ten faces, ten arms, ten feet, kohl-black shine, and thirty wide eyes strung like a garland.

Though of terrible form, O king — glittering teeth and fangs — She is the home of beauty, luck, glow and great fortunes. (Verse 4.) In simple words: yes, She looks fearsome with flashing fangs — yet that very form is where beauty, fortune, radiance and all riches live.

Bearing sword, arrow, mace, spear, conch, discus, sling — mace-staff, bow, and a head dripping blood She held. (Verse 5.) In simple words Her ten hands hold ten weapons: sword, arrow, mace, spear, conch, discus, fire-sling, iron club, bow — and a dripping severed head.

She is Viṣṇu's illusion, Mahākālī hard to cross; worshipped, She brings the moving world under the worshipper's sway. (Verse 6.) Combined with the commentaries: 'three-qualitied' means passion-chief with darkness-goodness as side-shades. 'With-Śarva' takes no feminine ending for lack of husband-sense. (Verse 1.) Then Mahākālī's other form: 'sleep-yoga' (2); three eyes per face is meant by 'thirty' (3–4); weapons in order from low-right hand to low-left: sword and the rest, 'head' is the skull-staff (5–6). The Hindi prayer repeats it whole: three-named Goddess — passion-Mahālakṣmī, dark-Mahākālī, bright-Mahāsarasvatī — hailed as Śarvā, Caṇḍikā, Durgā, Bhadrā, Bhagavatī (1); dark Mahākālī, Viṣṇu's sleep, praised by lotus-Brahmā against Madhu-Kaiṭabha (2); kohl-glow, ten faces, ten arms, ten feet, thirty-eye garland (3); O king, though terrible with glittering teeth-fangs, home of beauty, luck, glow and great fortunes (4); sword 1, arrow 2, mace 3, spear 4, conch 5 (with variants: discus 6, sling 7, and club 8, bow 9, and the ever-bleeding severed head 10 — held in ten hands) (5); this Viṣṇu-illusion Mahākālī, though unconquerable, worshipped, lays the moving world at the worshipper's feet (6).

From all the gods' bodies burst boundless-glory She — three-qualitied Mahālakṣmī Herself, the Buffalo-killer. (Verse 7.) In simple words the middle story's Queen steps out: born from every god's body-fire fused in one, endless in glory — Mahālakṣmī the three-powered, slayer of Mahiṣa in person.

White-faced, blue-armed, snowy-breasted, red-waisted; fair-footed, blue-thighed, proudly mad. (Verse 8.) In simple words Her strange beauty is painted limb by limb: white face, blue arms, snow-white breasts, red middle, red feet, blue thighs — drunk with unconquered pride.
Decked in bright garlands, robes and paints — beauty-luck-rich in form. (Verse 9.) In simple words: many-colored garlands, clothes and body-paints — radiance, beauty and fortune all in one body.

Eighteen-armed, worshipful — though thousand-armed in truth. Her weapons now are told, from low-right hand in order. (Verse 10.) In simple words: for worship count eighteen arms (though really She has a thousand) — and here comes the weapon-list, starting low-right, hand by hand.

Rosary and lotus, arrow and sword, thunderbolt and mace; discus, trident, axe, conch, bell and noose. (Verse 11, first twelve.) In simple words the first twelve in order: beads, lotus, arrow, sword, thunderbolt, mace, discus, trident, axe, conch, bell, noose.

Spear and staff, hide and bow, wine-cup and water-pot — with these weapons Her arms are graced, lotus-seated. (Verse 12, last six.) In simple words the last six: spear, staff, shield, bow, cup, flask — eighteen arms all weapon-bright, seated on a lotus.

This Mahālakṣmī, made of all gods, the Lady — O king, whoever worships Her becomes lord of worlds and gods. (Verse 13.) Combined with the commentaries: then Mahālakṣmī's changed form: 'from all gods' (verses 7–9); 'thousand-armed' really means endless-armed (10–13). The Hindi prayer repeats verses 7–13 whole: Mahiṣa-crusher Mahālakṣmī, three-powered, born of all gods' bodies (7); white face, blue arms, snowy breasts, red waist and feet, blue thighs, pride-mad (8); bright robes-jewels-paints, beauty-luck-rich (9); eighteen arms for worship though thousand-armed in truth, weapons told low-right onward (10): beads 1, lotus 2, arrow 3, sword 4, thunderbolt 5 (with variants: mace 6, discus 7, trident 8, axe 9, conch 10, bell 11, noose 12) (11); spear 13, staff 14, shield 15, bow 16, cup 17, flask 18 — weapon-graced arms, lotus-seated (12); worship this all-gods-made, all-mighty Mahālakṣmī, O king, and rule all worlds and gods (13). One book reads 'worshipping' and 'of all worlds' here.

From Gaurī's body rose She, resting on goodness alone — Sarasvatī Herself, killer of Śumbha-demons. (Verse 14.) In simple words the bright daughter's changed face: born from Fair Gaurī's body, pure goodness only — Sarasvatī in person, Śumbha's slayer.

Eight-armed She held arrow, club, spear, discus; corpse, bell, plough and bow too, O earth-lord. (Verse 15.) In simple words Her eight hands: arrow, club, spear, discus — plus corpse, bell, plough and bow.

Worshipped with love She grants all-knowing — Niśumbha-pounder, Śumbha-demon-ender Goddess. (Verse 16.) In simple words: love-worshipped, She gives total wisdom — grinder of Niśumbha, finisher of Śumbha.

Thus are told the faces of the forms, O king; now hear, apart, the world-Mother's worship. (Verse 17.) In simple words the sage closes the face-list and opens the worship-manual: faces told — now learn how to serve each, one by one.

When four-armed Mahālakṣmī is worshipped, Mahākālī-Sarasvatī right-left; behind, the three pairs. (Verse 18.) Combined with the commentaries: now Mahālakṣmī's worship: right-left split follows the worshipper. And in Her changed form, worship-modes: 'eighteen-armed' — right-left follows the Goddess, since 'Her' is stressed; though ten-faced has two faces per ten arms, when the chief goddess is served in second form the other two serve as limbs in second form too — but served in first form, they serve in first form. 'Great Lakṣmī' lacks a second-case ending, since 'thus' already says the object-hood. When the other two are served freely, with no fixed must-do, He tells only their shared threefold rite in verse-and-half: 'eighteen-armed' — 'right-left' joins what follows. In the gods' three free separate rites too, south holds Time, north Death — both deities to serve, is the sense. (Verses 18–22.) The Hindi prayer repeats it whole: worship four-armed Mahālakṣmī centre, four-armed Mahākālī right, Mahāsarasvatī left, and the three pairs behind (18).

Brahmā with Learning centre, Rudra with Gaurī right; with Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu left; before, the goddess-triad. (Verse 19.) In simple words the couple-seating: centre Brahmā-Learning, right Rudra-Gaurī, left Viṣṇu-Lakṣmī, and the three goddesses facing them in front.

Eighteen-armed centre, ten-faced left of Her, eight-armed Lakṣmī right — worship thus the Great One. (Verse 20.) In simple words the second seating: centre eighteen-armed Mahālakṣmī, left ten-faced Mahākālī, right eight-armed Mahāsarasvatī — worship the Great Goddess so.

And when the eighteen-armed is worshipped, O king of men — ten-faced and eight-armed right-left then. (Verse 21.) In simple words the free-standing rite: serve the eighteen-armed One alone, with ten-faced right and eight-armed left.

Time and Death both to be served, for all evils' calming; and when eight-armed Śumbha-killer is worshipped. (Verse 22.) Combined with the commentaries: the three pairs are seated place-wise — 'Brahmā and the rest' (19). Right-left follows the Goddess in Her changed-form modes (20); the second-form rule for limbs; and in free separate rites, Time south, Death north (21–22). The Hindi prayer continues: behind centre-Mahālakṣmī — Brahmā-Learning centre, Rudra-Gaurī right, Viṣṇu-Lakṣmī left, three goddesses in front (19); centre eighteen-armed, left ten-faced, right eight-armed — so serve the Great One (20); served freely apart, right and left of them… (21; Time and Death next).

Time south and Death north serve well, to calm all evils; when the eight-armed Śumbha-killer is served apart. (Verse 22, Hindi.) In simple words the devotee notes the two guardian extras — Time and Death — who keep every misfortune quiet.

Her nine powers be served, and Rudra-Vināyakas both; with 'salutation to Goddess' hymns, worship great Lakṣmī. (Verse 23.) In simple words: serve Her nine powers (Brāhmī and the eight sisters), Rudra right and Gaṇeśa left, chanting 'salutation to the Goddess' over great Lakṣmī.

In the three descents' worship, hymn-mantras stay with their homes; and eighteen-armed Buffalo-killer is worshippable. (Verse 24.) In simple words the mantra-rule: each descent is hymned with its own hymns — Mahākālī with 'You are Svāhā, You are Svadhā', Mahālakṣmī with 'the Goddess by whom all this is spread', Mahāsarasvatī with 'O Goddess who rescues the surrendered in pain' — and chief over all for Caṇḍī-praisers, daily and on wish-days, stands eighteen-armed middle-story Mahālakṣmī; the other two, served-or-not as you will. Since She is the Whole, serving Her nearly serves the other two — hence He describes Her alone at length. (Continued next.)

Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī — She alone is called Sarasvatī; Queen of merit and sin, great Queen of all worlds. (Verse 25.) Combined with the Hindi: on Her right serve Rudra, on Her left Vināyaka Gaṇeśa, plus Her nine powers — Brāhmī 1, Māheśvarī 2, Kaumārī 3, Vaiṣṇavī 4, Vārāhī 5, Nārasiṃhī 6, Aindrī 7, Śivadūtī 8, Cāmuṇḍā 9 — chanting 'salutation to the Goddess' over four-armed Mahālakṣmī (23). For the three descents use their own hymn-mantras — eighteen-armed for 'the Goddess by whom', ten-faced for the night-hymn, eight-armed for the Nārāyaṇī-hymn; Buffalo-killer eighteen-armed Mahālakṣmī is the special worship (24). For She alone is hailed Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, Sarasvatī — Queen ruling merit and sin, great Queen of all the worlds. (25.)

She alone is Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, Sarasvatī — ruler of merit and sin, great Queen of all worlds. (Verse 25, Hindi seal.) In simple words the oneness is driven home: three names, one Queen — over every deed, every world.

Who worshipped Buffalo-ender becomes world-lord; worship the world's nurse, Caṇḍikā, lover of devotees. (Verse 26.) In simple words the standing order: whoever served Mahiṣa-ender Lakṣmī has ruled worlds — so serve the world-nurse, devotee-loving Caṇḍikā.

With guest-gifts and the rest. (Verse 27, with an old quoted line.) Combined with the old note: 'with guest-gifts' — then offerings. In simple words the worship-ware list begins: welcome-water and the rest to follow.

With offerings of many eatables. (Verse 27, Hindi listing.) Combined with the old note: 'I' — then with many-eatables offerings. In simple words the food-offerings: many tasty dishes heaped before Her.

With blood-wet victim, flesh and wine, O king; with bow-water, sandal sweet-smelling. (Verse 28.) In simple words the fierce offerings: blood-smeared victim, meat and wine; sipping-water and sweet sandal.

With camphor betels, full of loving devotion; to the Goddess's left-front, the beheaded great demon. (Verse 29.) In simple words: camphor-rolled betel-leaves offered with love — and to Her left-front, the beheaded mighty demon (Mahiṣa) himself is worshipped.

Worship the buffalo — by whom union with the Lady was won; to the right-front, the lion — all-dharma, the Lord. (Verse 30.) In simple words: worship the buffalo too, for through Her it won oneness with the Goddess; and to Her right-front, the lion — dharma itself in full, the Lord's own form.

The Goddess's vehicle worship — by whom the moving world is held; whoever does, striving, wise, one-pointed in mind toward Her. (Verse 31.) Combined with Guptavatī's ritual grammar: verses 26–27 need nothing; on 'blood-wet' — victim-rules by brāhmaṇa and the rest were told before, not to be re-thought. (Verses 28–29.) The lion's vehicle-form is told: 'all-dharma' means the rite-acts taught by all fourteen lores. (Verse 30.) 'Whoever does Her worship' joins with what went before — he should worship the lion. (Verse 31.) The Hindi prayer repeats it whole: whoever served buffalo-ending Mahālakṣmī has been world-lord and shall be — so serve world-nurse, devotee-loving Caṇḍikā (26). Then Sumedhas tells the worship-mode, O king — with welcome-water and the rest, ornaments, scents, flowers, unbroken rice, lamp-incense, and many-eatables food-gifts (27); with blood-wet victim, flesh, wine, bowing and sipping water, sweet sandal (28); with loving camphor-betels and the rest. To the Goddess's left-front, that great demon of severed head (29) — worship Mahiṣa, who won union with the Lady. To Her right-front the lion — all-dharma itself, Lord-natured (30). The Goddess's vehicle, by whom the moving world is held. Then the wise man, striving, one-pointed toward Her, should hymn Her. (31.)

Then, folded hands become, praise with these stories — with one, or the middle; not with one of the other two here. (Verse 32, with verse 33 quoted.) Combined with the old note: 'but don't chant for story-fruit — chanting gaps wins a hole.' Then circling and bowing, folded hands on the crown. (Verse 33.) In simple words the praise-rule: palms joined, hymn Her with these stories — with all three, or with the middle one alone; never with just one of the other two. And never chant half a story for its fruit — a gapped chant earns a hole.

Beg pardon of the world-nurse again and again, untiring; verse by verse offer milk-rice with sesame-ghee. (Verse 34.) Combined with the commentaries: 'then' — after limb-god worship, praise with the fit three stories, or middle-story alone, or all four hymns — for where the earlier choice fails, the later choice stands settled. (Verses 32–33.) 'Verse by verse' marks one of the told mantra-shares; here some offer fire per verse of armour-trio and mystery-trio both — but in the armour share fire is unfit, another lore forbids it, as: 'in Caṇḍī-praise, one fire per verse is wished; with armour-hymn mantras make no fire there; from blindness, whoever fires per verse with armour-hymns — his body shall fall, he'll reach hell; the great demon Andhaka, set on Durgā-fire, fell by Mahādeva for armour-fire-born sin' — and more. (Verse 34.) The Hindi prayer repeats: palms joined, praise with these three stories — or the middle story alone, never one of the other two (32). Never do half a story — half-reading may win harm. Then circling and bowing, palms-to-crown pose (33). Untiring, beg the world-nurse pardon again and again for faults and slips; then with sesame-ghee milk-rice, chanting each verse-mantra, offer fire. (Verse 34, Hindi.)

Offer fair fire to Caṇḍikā with hymn-mantras or else; with 'salutation, salutation' words worship the Goddess, well-composed. (Verse 35.) In simple words: fire into Her flame with hymn-mantras — or else; then settled and calm, worship the Goddess chanting Her name-mantras with 'salutation, salutation'.

Striving, palms joined, humble — bowing, lifting Her into the self — long contemplate the Lady, Caṇḍikā, becoming Her. (Verse 36.) In simple words: striving, hands joined, bowing low, place all-goddess Caṇḍikā inside the heart and sit with Her long — until you become Her.

Who thus worships with love the supreme Lady day by day — enjoying wished joys as wished, he wins the Goddess's union. (Verse 37.) In simple words the daily fruit: love-worship Her every day — enjoy every wished joy to the full, then win oneness with the Goddess.

Who worships not daily Caṇḍikā, lover of devotees — burning his merits to ash, the supreme Lady burns. (Verse 38.) In simple words the warning: skip daily worship of devotee-loving Caṇḍikā, and the supreme Lady burns your merits to ash and ash.

So worship, O king! the great Queen of all worlds — by the told rule, Caṇḍikā — and you shall win joy. (Verse 39.) In simple words the sage closes: so worship Her, O king, world-Queen Caṇḍikā, exactly as told — and joy is yours.

Thus ends the Vaikṛta mystery. Combined with the closers: the other path is told for the less able — 'offer with hymn-mantras or else'; this fire-rite belongs to worship's limbs. (Verses 35–36.) Her wished-and-daily natures are told in turn by 'who thus' in two verses. (37–38.) 'So' concludes. (39.) Thus ends the Guptavatī on the Vaikṛta mystery. The Hindi prayer continues: or else fire fair offerings with hymn-mantras alone (some use all four praises, some use 'to Caṇḍikā salutation' alone for the fire-rite). After fire, calm-minded, worship great Lakṣmī again chanting Her name-mantras. (Verse 35, Hindi; continues: bowing, heart-lifting, oneness — next.)
After fire, worship again with name-mantras, calm-minded. (Verse 35, Hindi.) In simple words: fire done — sit still, chant Her names, worship again.

Then striving, palms joined, humble, bowing to the Goddess, lifting the all-Queen Caṇḍikā into the heart, contemplate long and grow into Her. (Verse 36, Hindi, with old note + variant.) Combined with the old note: whoever love-worships the supreme Lady daily enjoys wished joys and wins Goddess-union (37). Whoever worships not daily devotee-loving Caṇḍikā — his merits the supreme Lady burns to ash (38). So, O king, worship world-great-Queen Caṇḍikā by the told rule — and you shall win joy (39). One book reads 'again with name-words' and 'joys' here.

Blessed Nandā the Goddess, who shall be born of Nanda — praised and worshipped with love, She lays all three worlds at (the worshipper's) feet. (Mūrti verse 1.) In simple words the mystery of faces opens: the coming Goddess named Nandā, born of Nanda — love-serve Her and all three worlds come under your sway.

Of finest-gold glow, lovely-glow golden-robed Goddess — gold-hued, gloriously gold-decked. (Verse 2.) In simple words Nandā shines: finest gold Her glow, lovely gold Her robes, golden Her color, finest gold Her jewels.

Lotus, goad, noose, conch-graced, four-armed; Indirā, Kamalā, Lakṣmī — She, Fortune, lotus-golden-seated. (Verse 3.) In simple words Her four arms hold lotus, elephant-goad, noose and conch; and She is hailed Indirā, Kamalā, Lakṣmī, Fortune Herself, seated on a golden lotus.

The Goddess named Raktadantikā, O sinless, told by me — Her form I shall tell; hear, remover of all fears. (Verse 4.) In simple words the sage turns to the next face: sinless king, I told you of blood-toothed Raktadantikā — now hear Her form, which ends every fear.

Red-robed, red-hued, red-all-limbs-decked; red-weaponed, red-eyed, red-haired, most dread. (Verse 5.) In simple words She is red all over: red clothes, red color, red jewels on every limb, red weapons, red eyes, dread red hair.

Red sharp nails, red teeth — Raktadantikā; as a loving wife loves her lord, the Goddess loves Her worshipping folk. (Verse 6.) Combined with Guptavatī's grammar: now the seven faces from Nandā are worshipped in brief. 'With lotus-goad-noose' — lotus means conch, or lotus itself, since elsewhere in Lakṣmī-focus two lotuses in two hands are seen. (Verses 1–5.) 'As a wife her lord' is a likeness only in the loving part. (Verse 6.) The Hindi prayer repeats it whole: Nandā, born of Nanda, love-served, lays three worlds at feet (1); finest-gold glow, lovely gold robes, gold-hued, finest-gold-decked (2); four arms graced with lotus, goad, noose, conch — hailed Indirā, Kamalā, Lakṣmī, Fortune, golden-lotus-seated (3); O sinless king, now hear blood-toothed Raktadantikā's form, ender of all fears (4); red-robed, red-hued, red-jewelled everywhere, red-weapons, red eyes, dread red hair (5); sharp red nails, red teeth — hence Raktadantikā. (Continues: loving as a wife loves — next.)

As a loving wife loves her lord, so the Goddess loves Her devotees. (Verse 6, Hindi.) In simple words the tenderness is sealed: Her love for devotees is exactly a devoted wife's love for her husband — total and personal.

Vast as the earth, Her breasts twin Merus; long and hanging, over-plump, yet utterly charming. (Verse 7.) In simple words the cosmic-mother image: vast as earth, breasts like twin Meru peaks — long, hanging, full — and utterly lovely.

Hard yet most lovely, twin seas of all bliss — the Goddess feeds devotees the wish-cow breasts. (Verse 8.) In simple words: firm yet beautiful, oceans of all joy — with those wish-fulfilling breasts the Mother nurses Her devotees.

Sword and cup, club and plough She bears — hailed blood-Cāmuṇḍā, and Goddess queen of yogis. (Verse 9.) In simple words Her four hands: sword, wine-cup, club, plough — and She is hailed blood-Cāmuṇḍā, queen of all yogis.

By Her is pervaded the whole still-moving world; whoever worships Her with love pervades the moving world. (Verse 10.) In simple words: She fills everything still and moving — and whoever loves Her fills the moving world too.

Whoever daily reads this body-praise of blood-toothed (Raktadantikā) — the Goddess serves him as a wife serves a dear lord. (Verse 11.) In simple words the daily-reader's reward: chant Her body-praise every day, and the Goddess Herself serves you as a wife serves her beloved.

Śākambharī blue-hued, blue-lotus-eyed; deep-navelled, triple-fold graced slim-bellied. (Verse 12.) In simple words the next face: blue-complexioned, blue-lotus-eyed, deep-navelled, slim-waisted with three lovely folds.

Hard, matched, high, round, plump, full breasts; fist full of arrows, lotus — lotus-homed. (Verse 13.) Combined with the commentaries: verses 7–8 need nothing; 'cup' is the honey-drinking tool. (Verses 9–12.) 'Arrow-fists' — arrows: She bears bow-arrow-lotus-missiles in four hands, is the sense. (Verse 13.) The Hindi prayer repeats it whole: blood-toothed Goddess vast as earth, breasts twin Merus — long, hanging, over-plump, yet utterly charming (7); hard yet most lovely, seas of all bliss — with wish-cow breasts the Goddess feeds devotees (8); sword, cup, club, plough in four hands — hailed blood-Cāmuṇḍā, queen of yogis (9); by Her the whole still-moving world is pervaded; whoever loves Her pervades the moving world (10). (Continues: daily body-praise, Śākambharī's blue form — next.)

Daily body-praise wins Her wifely service; Śākambharī's blue lotus-eyes, deep navel, triple-fold slim waist. (Verses 11–12, Hindi.) Combined with the split notes: whoever daily reads this body-praise of blood-toothed Raktadantikā is served by the Goddess as a wife serves a dear lord (11); blue-hued Śākambharī, blue-lotus-eyed, deep-navelled, triple-fold graced slim-bellied (12). (Continues: hard matched breasts, arrow-fist, lotus — next.)

Flower, leaf, root and fruit-rich, a greens-heap — wished, endless-tasted — ending hunger, thirst, death, fever. (Verse 14.) In simple words Śākambharī the herb-bearer: heaps of greens — flowers, leaves, roots, fruits — of every wished taste, endless, curing hunger, thirst, death and fever.

Bow of shooting light bearing, supreme Lady — Śākambharī, hundred-eyed, She alone is famed Durgā. (Verse 15.) In simple words: bow of flashing light in hand — and know: hundred-eyed Śākambharī is Herself famed Durgā, by time-place-state names.

Sorrowless, wicked-tamer, calmer of sins and dangers — Umā, Gaurī, Satī, Caṇḍī, Kālikā too is Pārvatī. (Verse 16.) In simple words one garland of names: grief-free, punisher of the wicked, soother of sin and peril — Umā, Fair One, True One, Fierce One, Dark One — and all are Pārvatī.

Praising, picturing, chanting, worshipping, bowing Śākambharī — soon wins food-drink-deathless fruit, unending. (Verse 17.) In simple words the all-in-one promise: hymn Her, picture Her, chant Her, serve Her, bow to Her — and soon win food, drink and deathless fruit that never ends.

Terrible too, blue-hued — fang-tooth shining; wide-eyed woman, round full-breasted. (Verse 18.) In simple words the seventh face, Bhīmā: blue-bodied even in terror, fangs and teeth agleam, wide eyes, woman's form, round full breasts.

Moon-laugh (sword), drum, head-cup bearing — the One Heroine, Night-of-death, hailed wish-giver when praised. (Verse 19.) In simple words Her four hands: bright sword, little drum, skull-cup — hailed One Heroine and death-night, and praised, She grants every wish.

Hard to face through glory-orbed, bee-variegated, bright-hued; paint-pasted Goddess, bright-jewel-decked. (Verse 20.) Combined with the notes: the seventh face is told — 'glory' (verse 20). 'Moon-laugh' is the sword. (Verse 19.) On such spots only simile's shared ground is wanted, not full likeness — so the sage's point is just love's fullness. One book reads 'fear-remover' here. The Hindi prayer continues: greens-heaps of flower-leaf-root-fruit, endless-tasted, hunger-thirst-death-fever-ending (14); flashing bow in hand — the same Lady by time-place-state is Śākambharī, hundred-eyed, famed Durgā (15); sorrowless, wicked-taming, sin-peril-soothing — Umā, Gaurī, Satī (meant: Satī), Caṇḍikā, Kālikā and Pārvatī are all She (16); whoever hymns, pictures, chants, serves and bows Śākambharī soon wins food, drink and deathless unending fruit (17). (Continued: terrible blue Bhīmā — next.)

Whoever hymns, pictures, chants, serves and bows Her soon wins unending food-drink-deathless fruit. (Verse 17, Hindi.) In simple words: five-fold devotion — sing, see, chant, serve, bow — and deathless nourishment, forever, soon.

Terrible blue Bhīmā, fang-tooth agleam, wide-eyed woman, round full-breasted. (Verse 18, Hindi, with old note.) Combined with the old note: in four hands — moon-laugh, drum, head and wine-cup bearing. (Continues: One Heroine, death-night, wish-giver when praised — next.)

Moon-laugh, drum, head and cup in four hands — the One Heroine, death-night, wish-giver when praised. (Verse 19, Hindi.) In simple words: sword, drum, skull, cup — hail the lone heroine of death-night, and She fulfils every wish.

Bee-called Goddess, marvel-bright, glory-orbed unfaceable, many-painted, marvel-jewel-decked. (Verse 20, Hindi, with old note.) Combined with the old note: unfaceable through glory-orb, many body-paints, marvel-jewel-decked. (Verse 20.) In simple words: Bhrāmarī — shimmering many-hued, too bright to gaze at, painted and jewelled all over.

Wondrous-bee-handed, hailed great-plague — thus are told the Goddess's faces, O earth-lord! (Verse 21.) In simple words the face-list closes: marvel-bee in hand, hailed even as the great plague (that ends all plagues) — O king, so are the Goddess's faces told.

World-Mother Caṇḍikā's, when hailed — wish-cows; this top secret by you to none be told. (Verse 22.) In simple words: these faces of world-Mother Caṇḍikā, when hymned, are wish-cows granting every desire — but this topmost secret must never be told by you to anyone.

The god-faces' tale, read yourself, heedful; so with all effort chant the Goddess ceaselessly. (Verse 23.) In simple words the standing order: read this tale of divine faces yourself, carefully — and with every effort, chant the Goddess without a break.

By mere reading of mantras, from all sins — even seven-lives-gathered, priest-killing-like — one is freed. (Verse 24.) In simple words: just reading these mantras washes every sin — even priest-murder-grade sins piled over seven lifetimes.

The Goddess's focus, told by me — secret of secrets, great; so with all effort, giver of every wished fruit. (Verse 25.) In simple words: this focus of the Goddess I have told — most secret of secrets, and giver of every wished fruit — strive for it with all your strength.

Thus ends the Mūrti mystery. Combined with the closers: verses 21–22 need nothing; and the study of all three mysteries too is ordained — 'the tale' — heedful means sense-heedful, and all is blessed. (Verses 23–25.) One book reads 'wish-fruit-giver' here. Thus ends the Guptavatī on the Mūrti mystery. (Running page dust follows.) In simple words the book seals itself: study all three mysteries with heedful sense — all blessed.

For the four ancient seat-lines' joy, and to amaze the new — may my work stand. (Colophon verse 1.) In simple words the author's closing prayer for his own book: may it delight the old traditions and astonish the new.

Born in holy-shade, measured-joy-year, in mind-sky — may it spread holy-shade, measured-joy-year in mind-sky. (Colophon verse 2, chronogram.) In simple words a blessing in riddle-words hiding the work's birth-year: may it spread holy shade and measured joy in the sky of minds.

The teacher alone is Śiva — the teacher alone I serve; with the teacher alone I stand — salutation to the teacher. Naught is higher than the teacher — I am the teacher's child; may mind rest in the teacher, in victorious master-teacher. (Colophon verse 3.) In simple words the author's vow: teacher is Śiva, teacher is refuge, teacher is company — I am the teacher's child, salutation to the teacher.

By me — son of deep-voiced Bhāratī, Soma-drinking thinker of Kāśī-city, thrice-fire-piled — made as this Caṇḍī-praise brick-sacrifice: She who among Nandā and the rest is seventh, bee-faced, on terror's bank in our family-goddess field dwelling — may holy Candralā be pleased. (Colophon verse 4.) In simple words Bhāskararāya signs his work: a Kāśī scholar, thrice fire-sacrificer, built this commentary as a brick-altar of praise; and may our family Goddess — seventh among Nandā and the rest, bee-faced, dwelling by the terror-river in our holy field — holy Candralā, be pleased.

Thus ends the Guptavatī-named Saptashatī explanation, composed by thrice-fire-piled Bhāskararāya Bhāratī-Dīkṣita, son of all-Tantra-free master Gambhīrarāya Bhāratī-Dīkṣita, crown-jewel among word-proof-and-reason ocean-crossers. Salutation to Caṇḍikā, salutation salutation. 'Not to be given — from pity even to the poor-suffering-sick; deemed as saints' conduct, or else as duty.' (Verse 1, colophon seal.) In simple words the book closes with its author's full signature and one last guard-rule: this teaching is not to be handed out — not even from pity to the poor, sick or suffering — unless as saints' conduct, or else as duty.

Thousands of faults I do day and night; knowing 'this is my servant', forgive me, supreme Lady! (Pardon verse 1.) In simple words the poet's daily confession begins: day and night I pile up thousands of faults — but I am Your servant; knowing just that, forgive me, Mother Supreme.

I know not inviting, nor know I bidding farewell; nor know I worship's way — forgive, supreme Lady! (Pardon verse 2.) In simple words: I don't know how to call You, how to send You off, how to worship at all — forgive me anyway.

Mantra-less, rite-less, love-less, O queen of gods — whatever worship I did, O Goddess, let it stand full for me. (Pardon verse 3.) In simple words: my worship lacked mantra, lacked rite, lacked love — yet let it count as full, by Your grace making up every lack.

Having done a hundred faults, crying 'O Mother of the world!' — the goal he wins, not even Brahmā and the gods. (Pardon verse 4.) In simple words the wonder-promise: commit a hundred faults, then just cry 'Mother of the world!' — and win a goal even Brahmā and the gods cannot reach.

Faulty I am, sheltered in You, O Mother of the world; now I deserve mercy — do with me as You will. (Pardon verse 5.) In simple words total surrender: guilty, yes — but sheltered in You; now I am Yours to mercy; do whatever You wish with me.

Whatever was done less or more, unknowing, forgetting, erring — all of it forgive, O Goddess; be pleased, supreme Lady! (Pardon verse 6, Hindi.) Combined with the Hindi prayer: day and night I commit thousands of faults — knowing 'he is my servant', forgive them graciously (1); I know no inviting, no farewell, no worship-way — forgive (2); O Goddess, queen of gods, my mantra-less, rite-less, love-less worship — let it stand full by Your grace (3); doing a hundred faults yet crying 'Mother of the world' wins a goal beyond even Brahmā and the gods (4); O Mother of the world, I am faulty but sheltered in You — now deserving mercy, do as You will (5).

O Goddess, supreme Lady — whatever lack or excess I did unknowing, forgetting, erring — forgive it all and be pleased. (Verse 6, Hindi.) In simple words the last word: unknowing, forgetting, mistaking — however I fell short or overdid — forgive everything, and smile on me.

A page-header line preserved by the edition ('780 Durgāsaptaśatī'). The closing prayers flow around it: O bliss-bodied supreme Lady, Mother of the world, desire-Lady — lovingly accept this worship of mine and stay pleased (verse 7); keeper of secrets beyond secrets, take my offered chanting, grant me perfection by Your grace, O queen of gods (verse 8). To holy Durgā be the offering.

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: 'You are a devotee' — of both Goddess and guru, is the sense. At the book's start the religion-form truth was told — Brahman named by the word Caṇḍikā, the worshipped reality — and its three branch-forms Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, Mahāsarasvatī. So Caṇḍikā the fourth is the Whole itself, religion-shaped, beyond qualities — yet counted fifth. Since telling the three branches nearly tells their undivided Whole, the fourth, the text wordlessly drops the Whole and points instead to one of the branches as equal to the fourth in shelter-giving — calling it three-qualitied, formless, unseeable, dwelling within the three descents. (Continued next.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: The sage said to the king: this mystery you ask is top-secret — worth telling only in secret. (Continues next.)

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant: some read 'and twice-born'.

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: 'First of all' and the rest: the three-qualitied Whole of goodness-passion-darkness faces is itself the first cause of the whole expanse, say some. Others say Mahālakṣmī here is not one of the three branches but another name of the fourth, Caṇḍikā Herself — 'Śivā named Śakti, seated on Sadāśiva's lap, famed as Mahālakṣmī, rich in all gods' qualities,' says the Śiva Purāṇa. Not so: the Mahālakṣmī inside the sacrifices stands apart, being passion-heavy, praised through ten names, with no telling of the other two — so supplying extra words just to force that reading is painful twisting. 'Seen' means with qualities, 'unseen' means without qualities — Her grasping never shows, so She is called unseen; as the Goddess-Atharva-Top scripture says, She is knowledge whose object is Herself — knowledge that kills mere mind-knowledge. For 'I know this pot' ends in 'I', and though Brahman is reached by the last mind-wave, It is never reached as a fruit-object — that is the feeling.

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: The three-qualitied supreme Lady Mahālakṣmī, first of all… (continues next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Pointing to the 'seen': citron means the seed-filled fruit; 'shield' is hide, held in hands, supply that. Serpent and the other two She wears on the crown — 'emblem' here is Rudra's male mark, 'womb' Viṣṇu's female mark (for the Veda bids 'fashion a Viṣṇu-womb'), so by leftover logic the serpent must be Brahmā's mark. Thus She shows Herself as Brahmā-Viṣṇu-Rudra in one, male-female in one. Then the 'unseen': at world-dissolution the world rests as seed-habit without gross form — that She pervaded with Her glory, which is pure consciousness, is the sense. And that same Mahālakṣmī ripened further into Mahākālī-hood — 'seeing emptiness' (verses 7–8).

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: O king, four-armed Mahālakṣmī holds citron (sweet-lime fruit)… (continues next).

tikas.author: बिजौरा का फल
tikas.simpleEn: …mace, shield and wine-cup in hand… (continuation of the Hindi prayer of verse 5).

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: From Mahālakṣmī's dark share was born that woman — smooth like collyrium, with out-jutting splitter fangs lighting Her noble face, wide-eyed and slim-bodied. (Verse 8.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Head' means the neck-part set on a pole, the skull-staff; 'trunks' are headless bodies — supply 'on the chest'; She wears a trunk-garland on the chest and a head-garland on the head, is the sense. 'To Her spoke' — but some read the first and second persons swapped, making it the dark lady's sentence — wasted effort, that. For the latter-half 'give me name and deed, O Mother, salutation to You' is seen in many books — which rather unjoins it; so some people's case-split reading too is not to be taken. With no question from the goodness-natured one, the name-first answer ahead tells it. (Verses 9–11.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Four arms graced with sword, wine-cup, head and shield; trunk-garland on the chest, skull-garland on the head. (Verse 9.) Some books add here an extra verse — the dark finest lady asks Mahālakṣmī: 'give me name and deed, O Mother, salutation to You' — but since most books don't agree, it ranks as inserted. (Continues: Mahālakṣmī's naming speech — next.)

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant: some read 'wearing indeed a head-garland'. (Continues: Mahālakṣmī's ten-name speech — next.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: The ten names from Mahāmāyā onward are told soul-meaning-wise: 'these', says He. And the Kālī Purāṇa tells: the womb-wise being, pushed by birth-winds, born wisdom-less, She keeps yoking through past-life habits — into delusion, mine-ness, doubt at day's start, then hurling again and again into anger, checks, greed, then joining to lust, worry night and day, joylessness, vice-addiction — hence the world-Queen is hailed Great Illusion. And the Devī Purāṇa's name-meaning chapter gives the other names — seek them there. Name-chanting with such meaning-knowledge beforehand is what bears fruit. 'Through them' (verse 12). And that She ripened into Mahāsarasvatī-hood too: 'having spoken to Her' — and the verse 'these are yours' joins to that ten-name set as well. (Verses 13–14.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: These ten are your names, to prove true through your deeds in days to come; whoever learns your deeds through them, sings and reflects, will enjoy joy. (Verse 12.) O king, telling the dark Goddess so, Mahālakṣmī wore by purest goodness a second moon-bright form. (Verse 13, continues next.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Verse 15 needs nothing. 'In a pair a son and a daughter' — a brother-sister twin. (Verses 16.) 'Herself' here some explain as 'bearing Her own Śrī-named branch-form' — but for us who say Mahālakṣmī is the branch's very name, no such strain. (Verses 17–20.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Mahāvidyā 1, Mahāvāṇī 2, Bhāratī 3, Vāk 4… (continues next).

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: …5 Sarasvatī, 6 Āryā, 7 Brāhmī, 8 wish-cow, 9 Veda-womb, 10 queen of wisdom… (name-list fragment, continues next).

tikas.author: बुद्धि की ईश्वरी
tikas.simpleEn: …these ten shall be your names (verse 15). Then Mahālakṣmī bade Mahākālī and Mahāsarasvatī each bring forth a woman-man pair in their own likeness (16). So told, Mahālakṣmī Herself made a pair — both golden-wombed, lovely, lotus-seated (17). Then Mother Mahālakṣmī addressed the man as Brahman, Maker, Creator, Holder, and the woman as Fortune, Lotus, Lovely, Luck (18). Mahākālī and Mahāsarasvatī each made a pair too — 'their faces and names I tell you, Suratha' (19). Mahākālī bore a blue-throated, red-armed, white-limbed, moon-crested man, and with him a fair woman. (Verse 20, Hindi.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Triple lore and wisdom' — scholarly or not, each is a separate name-pair (verses 21–23). Having made three pairs, since weddings need bride-giving parents and no other men exist but themselves, they themselves took double-form, male-and-female both — 'thus' says so. Manhood Mahālakṣmī reached, Brahmahood Mahākālī, Rudrahood Mahāsarasvatī, Viṣṇuhood — is the sense. For though young women, they hold manhood too — not as two persons, nor half-and-half like the half-woman-lord, but both all-pervading, like sunlight and shade both filling the same bowl of water — that is the feeling. And this form is unseen to flesh-eyes, says 'the eyed': wisdom alone, fed by the teacher's nine-lettered grace, is the true eye — 'not knowing that' reads un-split. (Verse 24.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: He is Rudra-Śaṅkara-Still-Matted-Three-eyed; she is triple-lore-wisdom-wish-cow-speech-letter-note (21). O king, Mahāsarasvatī bore a fair woman and a dark man — hear both their names (22): Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Heart-Lord, All-Pervader, Man-Rescuer he; Umā, Gaurī, Satī, Caṇḍikā, Lovely, Lucky, Blessed she (23). Thus the three maidens at once became men too — the eyed (wisdom-given by the teacher) surely see it; others, not knowing this wisdom, cannot see. (Verse 24, Hindi.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Verse 25 needs nothing. The remaining creation is told: 'with Svarā joined' means met with triple-lore wisdom; 'that' — the egg-world of root-nature, ego and elements in order, the Sāṅkhya tattva-group (verses 26–27). 'Mahālakṣmī' — both Her formless and formed faces are Hers, not the other two's. So among the three branches, the Mahālakṣmī tinged with passion-chiefly usable two qualities, both-formed-and-formless, is the worshippable — that is the triple group. And to remove the doubt 'why are Mahālakṣmī's ten names barely sung if the branches matter most' — 'She alone' answers: since She alone gives names to the others, endless regress stops at the Giver needing no other giver — that is the 'alone'. (Verse 28.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: O king Suratha, Mahālakṣmī gave Learning to Brahmā, boon-Gaurī to Rudra, Fortune to Vāsudeva (25). With Learning Brahmā laid an egg; potent Rudra with Fair One split it (26). Inside, O king, came the root-cause brood — the whole five-element still-moving world (27). Then Keśava-Viṣṇu with Lakṣmī fed and guarded it all (and with Fair One the Great Lord later destroyed it all — a verse some books carry but the original here lacks). So, O king, Mahālakṣmī alone stands as Queen of all lords (other books: 'Mahālakṣmī the All-goodness Queen and All-Queen', verse 28).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: 'By other names' means by the other two branches' names alone — since the Fourth needs no separate names of Her own, that is the feeling. So with the Fourth quietly set aside, the Mahālakṣmī inside the three branches is the very best — that devotee-pride is the book's own natural intent. Hence the Saptashatī's four hymns: the Goddess-hymn praises the Fourth through the non-difference of Mahākālī and the other two; the other three hymns serve the three quality-faces in turn — that is the fine point. Others say the Fourth alone is worshippable and all three branches are low, and they painfully drag this book to say: Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, Mahāsarasvatī rule the three stories in turn, and the Fourth rules only the nine-lettered — but if the Saptashatī worshipped branches alone and never the Fourth, then the Lakṣmī-Tantra's Indra-dialogue (where ten descents are told from Mahālakṣmī first through Mahākālī to Bhrāmarī, closing with 'supreme is She, firm-set, greatly blest Mahālakṣmī, nature, supreme Lady; for Her praise Brahmā and all gods saw the Goddess-hymn, giver of all wished fruits; chanting it daily, crossing all pains, one wins great lordship; and Her descents with stories Vasiṣṭha told of old to King Suratha of the Svārociṣa age and to the surrendered merchant Samādhi') — all that would clash. For it proves the branch-dwelling Mahālakṣmī's firmness, Her non-difference, the Goddess-hymn's devotion to Her alone, and the three stories' devotion to Her through the branches — clarified by the Fourth Herself. So the whole Saptashatī is Mahālakṣmī wearing non-difference with the Fourth as supreme — which is why 'by one, or by the middle' allows the middle story alone as option for all three stories together — that is the direction. (Verse 29, end of Guptavatī on the Prādhāna mystery.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Mahālakṣmī alone is formless and formed, bearing many names — so She is knowable through those name-forms, and through no single other name. (Verse 29.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Three-qualitied' means passion-chief with darkness-goodness as side-shades. 'With-Śarva' takes no feminine ending for lack of husband-sense. (Verse 1.) Then Mahākālī's other form: 'sleep-yoga' (2); three eyes per face is meant by 'thirty' (3–4); weapons in order from low-right hand to low-left: sword and the rest, 'head' is the skull-staff (5–6).

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Sumedhas the sage said: the Goddess told as threefold — passion-Mahālakṣmī, dark-Mahākālī, bright-Mahāsarasvatī — is hailed as Śarvā, Caṇḍikā, Durgā, Bhadrā, Bhagavatī (1). Dark Mahākālī is Lord Viṣṇu's sleep-yoga, praised by lotus-Brahmā against Madhu-Kaiṭabha (2). Kohl-glow, ten faces, ten arms, ten feet, thirty-eye garland (3). O king, though terrible with glittering teeth-fangs, home of beauty, luck, glow and great fortunes (4). (Continues: ten weapons — next.)

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: …discus 6, sling 7, and club 8, bow 9, and the ever-bleeding severed head 10 — held in ten hands (5). This Viṣṇu-illusion Mahākālī, though unconquerable, worshipped, lays the moving world at the worshipper's feet. (Verse 6, Hindi completion.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Then Mahālakṣmī's changed form: 'from all gods' (verses 7–9); 'thousand-armed' really means endless-armed (10–13).

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Mahiṣa-crusher Mahālakṣmī, three-powered, born of all gods' bodies (7); white face, blue arms, snowy breasts, red waist and feet, blue thighs, pride-mad (8); bright robes-jewels-paints, beauty-luck-rich (9); eighteen arms for worship though thousand-armed in truth, weapons told low-right onward (10). (Continues: the eighteen — next.)

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variants: some read 'worshipping, of all gods' and 'of all worlds'. (Continues: beads, lotus, arrow… — next.)

tikas.author: वज्र
tikas.simpleEn: …thunderbolt 5 (with variants: mace 6, discus 7, trident 8, axe 9, conch 10, bell 11, noose 12) (11). (Continues: spear, staff, shield… — next.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Then Mahāsarasvatī's changed form: 'from Gaurī's body' (verses 14–16). Winding the first question's answer, He pledges the second question's answer: 'thus told' (17). Mahālakṣmī's worship: 'when Mahālakṣmī' — right-left split follows the worshipper. (Verse 18.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Resting on goodness alone, born of Fair Gaurī's body — Sarasvatī Herself, Śumbha's slayer (14). O earth-lord, eight arms holding arrow, club, spear, discus — plus corpse, bell, plough and bow (15). Love-served, this Sarasvatī grants total wisdom — Niśumbha-grinder, Śumbha-finisher (16). O king, thus the Goddess-faces' forms are told; now learn each world-Mother-face's worship apart (17). Worship four-armed Mahālakṣmī centre, four-armed Mahākālī right, Mahāsarasvatī left, and the three pairs behind (18).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: The three pairs are seated place-wise: 'Brahmā and the rest' (verse 19). And in Her changed form, worship-modes: 'eighteen-armed' — right-left follows the Goddess, since 'Her' is stressed; though ten-faced has two faces per ten arms, when the chief goddess is served in second form the other two serve as limbs in second form too — but served in first form, they serve in first form. 'Great Lakṣmī' lacks a second-case ending, since 'thus' already says the object-hood. (Verse 20.) When the other two are served freely, with no fixed must-do, He tells only their shared threefold rite in verse-and-half: 'eighteen-armed' — 'right-left' joins what follows. In the gods' three free separate rites too, south holds Time, north Death — both deities to serve, is the sense. (Verses 21–22.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Right behind centre-Mahālakṣmī: Brahmā-Learning centre, Rudra-Gaurī right, Viṣṇu-Lakṣmī left, and the three goddesses facing them in front (19). Centre eighteen-armed Mahālakṣmī (to the seer thousand-armed), left ten-faced Mahākālī, right eight-armed Mahāsarasvatī — so serve four-armed Mahālakṣmī (20). O king, when eighteen-armed Mahālakṣmī, ten-faced Mahākālī and eight-armed Mahāsarasvatī are served freely apart, then right and left of them… (21; continues: Time and Death — next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: More limbs for the eighteen-armed One's free worship: 'and when' — the nine powers are the Kavaca-told Śailaputrī-nine, or the seat-powers. 'Rudra' means right-left, is the sense. Then the rite-mantras: 'salutation' — by the single 'to the Goddess' or Atharva-top mantra; or 'to the Fierce' and all praise-mantras. (Verse 23.) 'In the three descents': Mahākālī with 'You are Svāhā, You are Svadhā' hymn-mantras, Mahālakṣmī with 'the Goddess by whom' hymn-mantras, Mahāsarasvatī with 'O Goddess who rescues the surrendered in pain' hymn-mantras — worship so, is the sense. Now for Caṇḍī-praise-servers the middle-story goddess eighteen-armed Mahālakṣmī alone is daily-and-wished worship; the other two, served-or-not as you will. Since She is the Whole, serving Her nearly serves the other two — to hum that expansion He describes Her alone at length. 'Eighteen-armed' and the rest. (Verses 24–25.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Then on their right serve Rudra, on their left Vināyaka Gaṇeśa, plus Her nine powers — Brāhmī 1, Māheśvarī 2, Kaumārī 3, Vaiṣṇavī 4, Vārāhī 5, Nārasiṃhī 6, Aindrī 7, Śivadūtī 8, Cāmuṇḍā 9 — chanting 'salutation to the Goddess' over four-armed Mahālakṣmī (23). For the three descents use their own hymn-mantras — eighteen-armed for 'the Goddess by whom', ten-faced for the night-hymn, eight-armed for the Nārāyaṇī-hymn; Buffalo-killer eighteen-armed Mahālakṣmī is the special worship (24). (Continues: She alone is all three — next.)

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: 'I' — then with many-eatables offerings. (Verse 27, Hindi listing fragment.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Verses 26–27 need nothing. On 'blood-wet': victim-rules by brāhmaṇa and the rest were told before, not to be re-thought. (Verses 28–29.) The lion's vehicle-form is told: 'all-dharma' means the rite-acts taught by all fourteen lores. (Verse 30.) 'Whoever does Her worship' joins with what went before — he should worship the lion. (Verse 31.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Whoever served buffalo-ending Mahālakṣmī has been world-lord and shall be — so serve world-nurse, devotee-loving Caṇḍikā (26). Then Sumedhas tells the worship-mode, O king — with welcome-water and the rest, ornaments, scents, flowers, unbroken rice, lamp-incense, and many-eatables food-gifts (27). (Continues: blood offerings, betel, buffalo and lion worship — next.)

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: But don't chant for story-fruit — chanting gaps wins a hole. Then circling and bowing, folded hands on the crown. (Verse 33.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Then' — after limb-god worship, praise with the fit three stories, or middle-story alone, or all four hymns — for where the earlier choice fails, the later choice stands settled. (Verses 32–33.) 'Verse by verse' marks one of the told mantra-shares; here some offer fire per verse of armour-trio and mystery-trio both — but in the armour share fire is unfit, another lore forbids it, as: 'in Caṇḍī-praise, one fire per verse is wished; with armour-hymn mantras make no fire there; from blindness, whoever fires per verse with armour-hymns — his body shall fall, he'll reach hell; the great demon Andhaka, set on Durgā-fire, fell by Mahādeva for armour-fire-born sin' — and more. (Verse 34.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Then palms joined, praise with these three stories — or the middle story alone, never one of the other two (32). Never do half a story — half-reading may win harm. Then circling and bowing, palms-to-crown pose (33). Untiring, beg the world-nurse pardon again and again for faults and slips; then with sesame-ghee milk-rice, chanting each verse-mantra, offer fire. (Verse 34, Hindi.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: The other path is told for the less able — 'offer with hymn-mantras or else'; this fire-rite belongs to worship's limbs. (Verses 35–36.) Her wished-and-daily natures are told in turn by 'who thus' in two verses. (37–38.) 'So' concludes. (39.) Thus ends the Guptavatī on the Vaikṛta mystery.

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Or else fire fair offerings with hymn-mantras alone (some use all four praises, some use 'to Caṇḍikā salutation' alone for the fire-rite). After fire, calm-minded, worship great Lakṣmī again chanting Her name-mantras. (Verse 35, Hindi; continues: bowing, heart-lifting, oneness — next.)

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: Contemplating long, growing into Her… (continues: daily fruit, warning, closing — next).

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variants: some read 'again with name-words' and 'joys'. (Continues: Mūrti mystery heads — next.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Now the worship of the seven faces from Nandā is told in brief. 'With lotus-goad-noose' — lotus means conch, or lotus itself, since elsewhere in Lakṣmī-focus two lotuses in two hands are seen. (Verses 1–5.) 'As a wife her lord' is a likeness only in the loving part. (Verse 6.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Sumedhas the sage said: O king, Nandā, born of Nanda, love-served, lays three worlds at feet (1). Finest-gold glow, lovely gold robes, gold-hued, finest-gold-decked (2). Four arms graced with lotus, goad, noose, conch — hailed Indirā, Kamalā, Lakṣmī, Fortune, golden-lotus-seated (3). O sinless king, now hear blood-toothed Raktadantikā's form, ender of all fears (4). Red-robed, red-hued, red-jewelled everywhere, red-weapons, red eyes, dread red hair (5). Sharp red nails, red teeth — hence Raktadantikā. (Continues: loving as a wife loves — next.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Verses 7–8 need nothing; 'cup' is the honey-drinking tool. (Verses 9–12.) 'Arrow-fists' — arrows: She bears bow-arrow-lotus-missiles in four hands, is the sense. (Verse 13.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Blood-toothed Goddess vast as earth, breasts twin Merus — long, hanging, over-plump, yet utterly charming (7). Hard yet most lovely, seas of all bliss — with wish-cow breasts the Goddess feeds devotees (8). Sword, cup, club, plough in four hands — hailed blood-Cāmuṇḍā, queen of yogis (9). By Her the whole still-moving world is pervaded; whoever loves Her pervades the moving world (10). (Continues: daily body-praise, Śākambharī's blue form — next.)

tikas.author: रक्तदन्तिका देवी की
tikas.simpleEn: …whoever loves Her pervades the moving world (10). (Continues: daily body-praise — next.)

tikas.author: शरीरवर्णन
tikas.simpleEn: …whoever daily reads this body-praise… (continues: Śākambharī's blue form — next.)

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: Old note (1 Guptavatī): on 14 — hundred-eyed, being no separate descent from Mother Durgā's face, only Her worship-rule is extended here. 'She alone' (verses 15–18). 'Moon-laugh' is the sword. (Verse 19.) The seventh face is told: 'glory' (verse 20).

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Greens-heaps of flower-leaf-root-fruit, endless-tasted, hunger-thirst-death-fever-ending (14). Flashing bow in hand — the same Lady by time-place-state is Śākambharī, hundred-eyed, famed Durgā (15). Sorrowless, wicked-taming, sin-peril-soothing — Umā, Gaurī, Satī (meant: Satī), Caṇḍikā, Kālikā and Pārvatī are all She (16). Whoever hymns, pictures, chants, serves and bows Śākambharī soon wins food, drink and deathless unending fruit (17). (Continues: terrible blue Bhīmā — next.)

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Poetics note: in such spots only simile's shared ground is wanted, not full likeness — so the sage's point is just love's fullness. Variant: some read 'fear-remover'. (Continues: wondrous-bee hand, wish-cow faces — next.)

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: …terrible blue Bhīmā… (18; continues: moon-laugh, drum, skull, cup — next).

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: …bee-called Goddess, marvel-bright… (20; continues: wondrous-bee hand — next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Verses 21–22 need nothing; and the study of all three mysteries too is ordained — 'the tale' — heedful means sense-heedful, and all is blessed. (Verses 23–25.)

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant: some read 'wish-fruit-giver'. (Page dust follows.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Wondrous-bee-handed, hailed great-plague — so are the Goddess's faces told, O king (21). World-Mother Caṇḍikā's faces, when hymned, are wish-cows granting every desire — but this topmost secret must never be told by you to anyone (22). So read this tale of divine faces yourself, carefully — and with every effort, chant the Goddess without a break (23). Daily reading of these mantras washes even priest-murder-grade sins of seven lives (24). So with all effort, the most-secret focus of the Goddess I have told — giver of every wished fruit (25).

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Day and night I commit thousands of faults — knowing 'he is my servant', forgive them graciously (1). I know no inviting, no farewell, no worship-way — forgive (2). O Goddess, queen of gods, my mantra-less, rite-less, love-less worship — let it stand full by Your grace (3). Doing a hundred faults yet crying 'Mother of the world' wins a goal beyond even Brahmā and the gods (4). O Mother of the world, I am faulty but sheltered in You — now deserving mercy, do as You will (5).

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: Old seal-verse: keeper of secrets beyond secrets, take my offered chanting, grant me perfection by Your grace, O queen of gods. (Verse 8.) 'To holy Durgā be the offering.' (Continues: bliss-bodied supreme Lady — next.)
